messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] stepwiseqtl identifies two QTLs in almost the same location
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] stepwiseqtl identifies two QTLs in almost the same location
messages.body_plain:
I would look at a plot of genotype for q3 and q4 jointly vs phenotype.

Often this sort of situation arises when there are a few outlying phenotypes that could be explained by a pair of QTL tightly linked in repulsion.

karl

> outsw1<-stepwiseqtl(x, max.qtl=8, penalties=pen, verbose=FALSE, pheno.col=2)

> q1- pos 47 chr E
> q2 pos 82 chr E
> q3 pos 117 chrE
> q4 pos 117.672 chr E
> q5 pos 8 chr X
>

>
> Thanks!
> Sarah

messages.body_plain:
Thank you! Yes, in inspecting the genotypes at those markers I found two individuals who were outliers with respect to their phenotype/genotype combination. I believe they are errors, and removing them removed the problem.

Stepwiseqtl does seem to detect a lot of qtls, even using strict penalties. Running it without those two individuals still yeilds:
summary(outsw)
  QTL object containing imputed genotypes, with 128 imputations.

      name chr      pos n.gen
Q1  E...@49.0   E  49.0000     3
Q2  E...@82.9   E  82.8651     3
Q3  E...@93.0   E  93.0000     3
Q4 E...@116.2   E 116.2404     3
Q5   X...@8.0   X   8.0000     2
Q6   C...@3.1   C   3.1105     3

I am pretty suspicious of this result, do you have any recommendations for supporting these qtls?

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] stepwiseqtl identifies two QTLs in almost the same location
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] stepwiseqtl identifies two QTLs in almost the same location
messages.body_plain:
The percent variance explained is simply a transformation of the LOD scores.  It's not particularly trustworthy in any case, but for linked QTL the values are misleading/wrong.  I've not figured out a good way to calculate such percent variance explained for linked QTL.

I'm not quite sure what you mean by "Shouldn't the variance accounted for by one of these QTL be placed on the other rather than attributing nearly equal effects to two so closely linked loci?"

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] ANOVA loop
messages.body_plain:
Say y is a phenotype of length n and X is a matrix of genotypes of dimension n x p.

  pval <- apply(X, 2, function(gen,phe)
                  anova(aov(phe ~ gen))[1,5], y)

You may need to use as.factor(gen), as follows:

  pval <- apply(X, 2, function(gen,phe)
                  anova(aov(phe ~ as.factor(gen)))[1,5], y)

As a for loop:

  pval <- rep(NA, ncol(X))
  for(i in 1:ncol(gen))
    pval[i] <- anova(aov(y ~ as.factor(X[,i])))[1,5]

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] FindDupMarkers output
messages.body_plain:
As it says in the help file, the output of findDupMarkers is list of marker names; each component is a set of markers whose genotypes match [each other and] one other marker, and the name of the component is the name of the marker that they match.

For example:

  data(hyper)
  findDupMarkers(hyper)

Gives the output:

    $D4Mit53
    [1] "D4Mit89"

    $D4Mit80
    [1] "D4Mit81"

    $D17Mit57
    [1] "D17Mit113"

    $D17Mit23
    [1] "D17Mit45"

D4Mit89 is duplicate of D4Mit53; D4Mit81 is a duplicate of D4Mit80, etc.

Duplicate markers are grouped together.  For each group, one is used as the name of the group, and the others form a component of the output.

In the above output, the duplicate markers are in pairs.  As an illustration, we can force a third marker into one of the groups by pasting over its genotype data.

  hyper$geno[[4]]$data[,"D4Mit276"] <- hyper$geno[[4]]$data[,"D4Mit80"]
  findDupMarkers(hyper)

gives the output

    $D4Mit53
    [1] "D4Mit89"

    $D4Mit81
    [1] "D4Mit80"  "D4Mit276"

    $D17Mit113
    [1] "D17Mit57"

    $D17Mit45
    [1] "D17Mit23"

So now D4Mit81, D4Mit80 and D4Mit276 form a group of three duplicate markers.

karl

messages.subject: scanone() parameters for non-normal phenotype
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

The data that I'm working with (bgonly) has a phenotype distribution (lifespan) that is not normal (plot is attached). It is coded as an F2 intercross, although I manually converted all BB genotypes to AB so that there is only AA and AB genotypes, (based on previous data, we expect little phenotypic difference between genotypes AB and BB).

My question is what parameters you think we should use for scanone(). I've tried setting the phenotype distribution to normal and binary (with >280days as the cutoff). This results in a rather lopsided binary curve though. I've also played around with not binary-izing the genotypes. However, none of these settings give me significant loci. I know it's quite possible that our data just does not contain significant loci, but I wanted to ask for any advice you have before throwing in the towel.

Another question is, how valid would it be to use a t.test() in R to evaluate my phenotype values vs. my two genotype groups, in place of the marker regression method in scanone() ? (No assumptions of phenotype distribution go into this.) Someone else in my group did this and got lower p-values than what scanone() returns.

Thank you so much for your help!

Best,

Elisa
